subject: English
topic: Direct and indirect speech — mixed tiers
description: Converting between direct quoted speech and reported speech

questions.stem: Change to indirect speech: He said, 'I am happy.'

options.option_text: He said that I am happy.
He said that he was happy.
He says that he was happy.
He said he is happy.

questions.explanation: Indirect speech — reporting verb in past tense → back-shift the tense in the reported clause (present → past). 'I am happy' → 'he was happy'. First-person pronoun 'I' → third-person 'he'. Add 'that' (optional but standard in writing). Only when the reporting verb is present tense ('He says that …'), tenses don't back-shift.
questions.subject: English
questions.topic: Direct and indirect speech — mixed tiers

questions.stem: Change to indirect speech: She said to me, 'Please help me.'

options.option_text: She told me to help her.
She said to me help her.
She said me that please help her.
She told me that she helped me.

questions.explanation: Requests / commands — change the reporting verb to 'told / asked / requested / ordered' + infinitive (to + V). 'Please' is dropped (politeness is already implicit in 'requested / asked'). Pronouns shift accordingly: 'me' (direct) → 'her' (indirect). 'She said to me' → 'She told me' (the 'to me' becomes the indirect object of 'told').

questions.stem: Change to indirect speech: She asked, 'Are you coming with me?'

options.option_text: She asked whether I was coming with her.
She asked that I am coming with her.
She asked me are you coming with her.
She told me I was coming with her.

questions.explanation: Yes/No questions — use 'if' or 'whether' in indirect speech; verb order becomes statement order (not inverted). 'Are you coming' → 'I was coming'. Pronouns: 'you' → 'I' (if reporting a question asked of 'me'), 'me' → 'her'. Remove the question mark — it becomes a statement.

questions.stem: Change to indirect speech: Ravi said, 'I will visit Delhi tomorrow.'

options.option_text: Ravi said that he will visit Delhi tomorrow.
Ravi said that he would visit Delhi the next day.
Ravi said he visits Delhi tomorrow.
Ravi said that he visited Delhi yesterday.

questions.explanation: Tense back-shift: 'will' → 'would'. Time expressions also shift: 'tomorrow' → 'the next day' / 'the following day'. Similar shifts — 'today' → 'that day', 'yesterday' → 'the previous day' / 'the day before', 'now' → 'then', 'here' → 'there', 'this' → 'that'. Pronoun 'I' → 'he'.

questions.stem: Change to indirect speech: He said, 'The sun rises in the east.'

options.option_text: He said that the sun rose in the east.
He said that the sun rises in the east.
He says that the sun rose in the east.
He said the sun will rise in the east.

questions.explanation: Universal truths, scientific facts, habitual actions DO NOT back-shift even when the reporting verb is past. 'The sun rises in the east' is a universal truth, so it stays in present tense. Same applies to 'Water boils at 100 °C', 'India gained independence in 1947' (historical fact with definite date). Proverbs, adages similarly.

questions.stem: Change to indirect speech: The teacher said, 'Don't be late.'

options.option_text: The teacher said that we are not late.
The teacher told us not to be late.
The teacher ordered don't be late.
The teacher said we should not late.

questions.explanation: Negative commands / prohibitions — 'told / ordered / warned + object + NOT TO + V'. 'Don't be late' → 'told us not to be late'. For positive commands, 'to + V' (without 'not'). The verb choice ('told / ordered / warned / forbade') depends on the tone.

questions.stem: Change to indirect speech: She said, 'What a beautiful day!'

options.option_text: She said that what a beautiful day it was.
She exclaimed that it was a very beautiful day.
She told that what a beautiful day.
She said it is a beautiful day.

questions.explanation: Exclamations — use 'exclaimed / cried out / shouted' + 'that' + expression in declarative form. 'What a X' / 'How X' becomes 'a very X' or 'so X'. 'Oh!' → 'exclaimed with sorrow / surprise / joy'. Exclamation mark is dropped.

questions.stem: Which is the correct indirect speech for: Rohan said, 'I have completed all my assignments.'?

options.option_text: Rohan said that he has completed all his assignments then
Rohan said that he had completed all his assignments
Rohan told that he had completed all my assignments
Rohan said that he completed all his assignments already

questions.explanation: B is correct: present perfect 'have completed' backshifts to past perfect 'had completed', and pronouns 'I'/'my' change to 'he'/'his'. Option A incorrectly retains 'has' without the obligatory backshift. Option C wrongly keeps 'my' instead of changing it to 'his', and 'told that' is non-standard for declarative indirect speech.

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect speech: The interviewer asked the candidate, 'What is your name?'

options.option_text: The interviewer asked the candidate what is your name
The interviewer asked the candidate that what his name was
The interviewer asked the candidate what his name was
The interviewer asked the candidate what was his name

questions.explanation: C is correct: WH-questions in indirect speech use normal subject-verb order (no inversion), omit 'that', backshift 'is' to 'was', and change 'your' to 'his'. Option D retains the inverted word order 'what was his name' — a very common exam error. Option B wrongly inserts 'that' before a WH-word, which is not permitted in indirect questions.

questions.stem: Which is the correct indirect speech for: Priya said to her manager, 'I can complete this task before the deadline.'?

options.option_text: Priya told her manager that she can complete this task before the deadline
Priya told her manager that she could complete the task before the deadline
Priya told her manager that I could complete this task before the deadline
Priya said to her manager that she could completed the task before deadline

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'can' backshifts to 'could', the pronoun 'I' changes to 'she', and demonstrative 'this' changes to 'the'. Option A fails to backshift 'can' to 'could'. Option C correctly applies 'could' but wrongly retains first-person 'I' instead of changing it to 'she'. Option D has the grammatical error 'could completed' — a double verb form.

questions.stem: Identify the correct indirect speech for: The coach said, 'You must practice daily if you want to improve.'

options.option_text: The coach said that he must practice daily if he wanted to improve
The coach said that he had to practice daily if he wanted to improve
The coach said that he must practice daily if he wants to improve
The coach said that he would practice daily if he wanted to improve

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'must' expressing personal obligation changes to 'had to' when the reporting verb is past tense; 'want' also backshifts to 'wanted'. Option A retains 'must', which is acceptable only for universal/logical necessity — not for personal obligation as here. Option C retains 'must' and also fails to backshift 'wants'. Option D substitutes 'would', which replaces obligation with mere willingness, distorting the original meaning.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly converts to indirect speech? Amit said to Seema, 'I will return your book tomorrow.'

options.option_text: Amit told Seema that he will return her book tomorrow
Amit told Seema that he would return her book the next day
Amit told Seema that he would return her book the following morning
Amit told Seema that I would return your book the next day

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'will' backshifts to 'would', 'tomorrow' changes to 'the next day', 'I' to 'he', and 'your' to 'her'. Option A fails both the modal backshift and the deictic time-shift. Option C correctly shifts the modal but alters 'tomorrow' to 'the following morning', which adds a meaning ('morning') not present in the original. Option D correctly shifts the time reference but retains first-person pronouns 'I' and 'your'.

questions.stem: Which is the correct indirect speech for: The doctor said, 'The patient may recover if he follows the prescribed diet.'?

options.option_text: The doctor said the patient might recover if he followed the prescribed diet
The doctor said the patient may recover if he follows the prescribed diet
The doctor said the patient might recover if he had followed the prescribed diet
The doctor said the patient would recover if he had followed the prescribed diet

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'may' (possibility) backshifts to 'might', and the present tense 'follows' in the conditional clause backshifts to simple past 'followed'. Option B applies no backshift at all. Option C — the most tempting distractor — correctly backshifts 'may' to 'might' but over-shifts 'follows' to past perfect 'had followed', which would imply an unfulfilled third-conditional meaning absent from the original. Option D changes 'may' to 'would', replacing possibility with certainty.

questions.stem: Which is the correct indirect speech for: She said to him, 'I wish you were with me here now.'?

options.option_text: She told him that she wished he was with her there then
She told him that she wishes he were with her here now
She told him that she wished he were with her there then
She told him that she had wished he had been with her here then

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'wish' backshifts to 'wished'; the subjunctive 'were' is retained as 'were' because subjunctive mood does not backshift in standard grammar; 'I'→'she', 'me'→'her', 'here'→'there', 'now'→'then'. Option A is the classic exam trap — it replaces subjunctive 'were' with indicative 'was', losing the mandatory subjunctive mood. Option B fails to backshift 'wishes' to 'wished'. Option D over-shifts to past perfect 'had been' and incorrectly retains 'here' instead of changing it to 'there'.
